content: Bioethics examines moral dimensions of biology, medicine, and healthcare, applying ethical principles to increasingly complex technological and social questions. Several fundamental principles guide bioethical analysis: autonomy respects individuals' rights to make their own informed decisions; beneficence promotes actions that benefit others; non-maleficence avoids causing harm (primum non nocereâ"first, do no harm"); and justice distributes benefits and burdens fairly across society. During public health emergencies like pandemics, these principles often conflict, creating ethical dilemmas. Resource allocation during scarcity presents particularly challenging questionsâwhether distributing ventilators, medications, vaccines, or healthcare worker time. Different frameworks suggest varying approaches: utilitarian perspectives aim to maximize overall benefit, potentially prioritizing those with better survival chances or longer remaining life expectancy; egalitarian approaches emphasize equal access regardless of social status, wealth, or other factors; and prioritarian views focus on helping the worst-off or most vulnerable populations first. Procedural justice becomes crucial when substantive answers remain contested, requiring transparent, inclusive, and consistent decision-making processes that stakeholders can accept as fair even when disagreeing with outcomes. Triage protocols formalize these approaches, establishing criteria for categorizing patients and allocating resources during crisesâideally developed prospectively rather than during emergencies, with community input and clear communication. Privacy and surveillance concerns emerge during public health responses, balancing disease tracking needs against confidentiality and autonomy through measures like contact tracing, quarantine enforcement, or digital monitoring. Research ethics during emergencies address questions like acceptable risk levels for experimental treatments, appropriate consent procedures during crises, and equitable distribution of research benefits across populations. International cooperation raises additional considerations including global justice, equitable vaccine and treatment access, and respecting cultural differences while maintaining core ethical commitments.

scenario.title: Pandemic Ethics Simulator
scenario.content: Students manage public health responses to a fictional pandemic, making resource allocation and policy decisions that raise challenging bioethical questions. The simulation presents limited resources (hospital beds, ventilators, medications, vaccines) alongside diverse community needs across different population groups. Students must develop and apply ethical frameworks to make decisions about triage protocols, quarantine policies, privacy limitations, research priorities, and international cooperation. The system tracks outcomes including lives saved, quality of life impacts, economic effects, and public trust levels across different community segments. Interactive tools allow students to explore perspectives from various stakeholders including patients, healthcare workers, vulnerable populations, and policy makers. Challenge scenarios introduce ethical dilemmas with no perfect solutions, requiring students to balance competing values, justify their reasoning, and communicate decisions to affected communities. Advanced features incorporate ethical theories, historical precedents, and cultural contexts to enrich decision analysis.

hypothesis.description: Students will apply bioethical principles by analyzing complex healthcare resource allocation scenarios. They will evaluate how different ethical frameworks lead to varying decisions in crisis situations, and develop principled approaches to resolving moral dilemmas that respect multiple values and stakeholder perspectives.
